pages.text:
*Sky Report: overcast, a lid of grey, whispers on every branch.*

By the time the moon had thinned to a sliver, the whole hedge knew. Whispers rustled through the hawthorns, the story changing shape three times over, though the core remained: Pip had flown, and she had stayed in the air.

She landed on her usual branch, the one with the best view of the sky and the worst view of the ground. Uncle Dorn was already there, waiting with feathers on end, a plume of grey and brown fluff that made him look twice his size. He did not turn around, nor did he blink.

"Where were you?" he asked, his voice low, scraping against the quiet night.

Pip’s chest felt tight, like a knot in a shoelace she couldn’t untie. She looked at the stars, then at his back, knowing there was no hiding there, not with Dorn.

"The fields," she said. "The Windmill Fields."

He turned then, slowly, his eyes wide and wet in the moonlight. "And Tuck?"

Pip nodded. She told him everything: the oak, the lessons, Nettle’s secret joining, and the spiral she had managed in the gust. She told it all because lying to Dorn felt like swallowing a pebble. He listened without interrupting or grumbling, and when she finished, he stared at the dark hedge, his chest heaving slightly, as if the effort of holding still had finally broken him.
pages.image: A tiny brown-streaked sparrow with a crooked left tail feather stands on a branch facing a plump, gloomy grey sparrow with feathers on end, under a starry night sky in a dark hedge.

pages.text:
Dorn’s voice cracked when he finally spoke. It was a thin, sharp sound, like a twig underfoot.

"I lost your parents to a storm," he said. The words fell into the silence between them, heavy and cold. "Storm-Sparrows fly into the edge of them. They ride the teeth of the wind. I cannot lose you, Pip. I cannot."

He stepped closer, his plump body blocking the moonlight. "I am not saying you are not good. I am saying you are mine."

Pip felt a lump in her throat, thick and stubborn. She pressed against his soft, grey feathers. She loved him fiercely, with a love that ached in her small bones. But she also felt the sky above, vast and waiting.

"If I stay low all my life," she whispered, her voice trembling, "I will be safe. And I will not be me."

Dorn closed his eyes. A single tear slid down his beak. He did not argue. He simply wrapped his wing around her, a tight, warm shield against the cold night air, and held on as if letting go would break the world.
pages.image: A plump grey sparrow tucks a tiny brown sparrow with a crooked tail feather close under his wing on a branch, his eyes closed tightly, while a sliver of moon shines through the dark leaves.

pages.text:
At dawn, the light was the color of old bone. Pip was summoned to the Gathering Rock. Elder Marra waited at the top, perched on a ledge of rough stone. She looked tired, her grey streaks dull, her torn wing tip drooping. The air was still, heavy with the promise of rain.

Marra’s voice boomed, but it was quiet underneath. "I saw the spiral. From the ridge. It was remarkable, for a chick of this size."

Pip puffed out her chest, trying to stand taller. "Thank you, Elder."

"But the Trial is dangerous. The rules are old." Marra’s eyes were hard, flinty. "Storm-Sparrows are built, not wished. You are not built for it, Pip. You will not enter."

Pip’s head tilted. "What do I have to do to be built?"

Marra opened her beak. Closed it. Looked out over the sleeping hedge. She could not answer. The silence stretched, thin and tight, until it snapped. Marra turned her back, a final, sharp gesture. "Go."

Pip did not go. She stood there, small and brown, looking up at the bird who held the keys to the sky. Marra did not look back.
pages.image: A tiny sparrow with a crooked tail feather looks up at a large, grey-streaked elder sparrow with a torn wing tip standing on a rocky ledge at dawn, with a misty hedge in the background.

pages.text:
Pip walked away with her chin high, though her eyes were wet and her wings felt heavy, dragging at her sides like wet wool. She flew low, skimming the tops of the reeds until she reached the Lightning Oak, where the hollow smelled of dry leaves and old rain.

Old Tuck was there. He was stripping bark from a twig with his beak, tapping it against the wood with a rhythmic click, click, click. He did not look up.

"Marra said no," Pip said. Her voice was flat.

Tuck stopped tapping. He looked at her with his one good eye. He did not offer comfort. He did not offer pity. He just watched her.

"So?" he said.

Pip blinked. "So?"

"The rule says you can't enter," Tuck said, dropping the twig. "Did the rule say you can't fly the course?"

Pip stared at him. The words hung in the air, simple and impossible. Tuck shrugged his ragged shoulders, a gesture so casual it seemed almost rude.

"I've broken worse," he said, and went back to whittling.
pages.image: A one-eyed, ragged old sparrow whittling a twig in a dark tree hollow while a tiny sparrow with a crooked tail feather looks at him with wide, shocked eyes.

pages.text:
From the ivy wrapped around the oak, a small voice squeaked. Nettle was there, her big eyes reflecting the dim light. She had been listening.

"The Trial is the day after tomorrow," Nettle whispered. Her feet twitched with nervous energy. "The course is the three winds: the Windmill Fields, the Salt Marsh, and the Cliffs of Calder."

Tuck looked up. Pip looked at Nettle.

"If we go before the entrants," Nettle continued, her voice gaining a tiny bit of strength, "we fly it first."

Pip looked at the sky. Dawn was coming, thin and pink, bleeding across the horizon. The wind was picking up, cool and sharp. It pulled at her feathers, inviting her. She looked at Tuck, then at Nettle. The fear was there, but so was the sky.

"We fly it first," Pip said.
pages.image: Three sparrows, one tiny with a crooked tail, one skinny and freckled, and one old and ragged, look up at a thin pink dawn sky from a tree hollow, with ivy wrapping the trunk.
